nameStory: The "mustard" in this lichen's name comes from its distinctive yellowish-green color that resembles prepared mustard spread. The "kidney" part refers to the kidney-shaped lobes that make up its leafy body, giving it a chunky, rounded appearance that's quite different from other foliose lichens.
description: Mustard Kidney Lichen is a medium-sized foliose (leafy) lichen that forms distinctive kidney-shaped patches on tree bark. It has a smooth, somewhat leathery texture with a characteristic mustard-yellow to olive-green color that becomes more vibrant when wet. The lichen typically grows 2-4 inches across, with thick, rounded lobes that feel substantial to the touch. This uncommon species creates eye-catching patches that stand out against dark bark.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Distinctive mustard-yellow to olive-green color that brightens considerably when wet, becoming almost lime-green; dry specimens appear more muted yellow-brown

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Foliose (leafy) with thick, kidney-shaped lobes that feel leathery and substantial when touched; lobes are broadly rounded rather than finger-like

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Upper surface is remarkably smooth and somewhat glossy, lacking the powdery coating or bumps found on many other lichens; feels like soft leather

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on the bark of deciduous trees, particularly maples and birches; rarely if ever on conifers or rocks

idTips.label: Underside
idTips.description: Lower surface is pale brown to whitish with scattered small bumps (cyphellae) that feel slightly rough to the fingertip

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches typically 2-4 inches across, though older specimens can reach 6 inches; lobes are thick and chunky rather than delicate

habitat: Found on the bark of mature deciduous trees in humid, old-growth or near-old-growth forests throughout New England's mountains and cooler valleys. Prefers the protected north sides of large maples, birches, and occasionally ash trees where moisture lingers. Most commonly encountered at elevations above 1,000 feet where air quality is high and humidity remains consistent.

seasonality.spring: Color begins to intensify as humidity increases; wet specimens show brilliant lime-green coloration that makes identification easier.
seasonality.summer: May appear more muted and yellowish during dry spells, but summer rains bring out the characteristic mustard-green color beautifully.
seasonality.fall: Excellent time for identification as increased moisture from fall rains keeps the lichen colorful while deciduous leaves don't obstruct tree trunk views.
seasonality.winter: Color remains visible but may be more subdued; snow melt and winter moisture can still bring out the characteristic green tones on warmer days.

funFact: This lichen is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only once in recent surveys, making it rarer than finding a four-leaf clover in your backyard - if you discover one, you're likely looking at something that fewer than a dozen people in the region have ever seen!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other kidney lichens, but the smooth, mustard-colored surface sets it apart - other kidney lichens tend to be grayer or have powdery, bumpy surfaces. Remember: "smooth as mustard" for this species versus "powdery like parmesan" for its cousin, Powdery Kidney Lichen.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of this species in New England means that any sighting should be photographed and reported to local naturalist groups or iNaturalist, as it could represent an important range extension or population discovery that contributes to our understanding of lichen distribution in the region.
compareHints: Unlike its relatives in the kidney lichen group, Mustard Kidney Lichen has a distinctly smooth upper surface and yellowish coloration. Powdery Kidney Lichen has a grayish, powdery surface coating, while Fringed Kidney Lichen has distinctive hair-like projections around its edges. The smooth, mustard-colored surface of this species is its signature feature that separates it from all other kidney lichens in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Powdery Kidney Lichen is smaller and more powdery than its relatives in the Nephroma genus.
Compared to its relatives like powdery kidney lichen and naked kidney lichen, fringed kidney lichen is the only one with those distinctive hair-like fringes along the lobe edges.
Unlike Powdery Kidney Lichen which is covered in soredia (powdery reproductive structures) that rub off on your fingers, Naked Kidney Lichen has a completely smooth, clean surface.
